newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russian fur producers face problems but no protests.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian fur producers face problems but no protests.

text.p: As long as the sun is shining, Grisha is safe. But in a few months, when the snow starts falling, his young life will end.
Grisha is a 12-week-old sable and he -- or rather his lustrous dark brown fur -- is one of the more precious commodities Russia has to offer.
Chances are good that next year his pelt will be used in a fur coat and be seen on the streets of Moscow, New York or Tokyo.

Grisha will not escape his destiny. Russian fur farms, once a flourishing business bringing hard currency into the former communist country, now face huge problems. But anti-fur protests are not among them.

"Our winters are hard and long and they will continue to be hard and long," said Alexander Kovalyenko, chief technician at the Zoltikovsky fur farm where Grisha resides. "When a Russian woman sees a fur she wants to buy it, not to spray on it."

In Russia, where temperatures of minus 30 degrees Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit) are not unusual and where winter in some places might last seven months, furs are generally considered a necessity, not a crime against nature.
Russia saw its first, and so far only, anti-fur demonstration last September when some naked, mainly foreign, activists showed up on Moscow's Red Square. They got a frosty reception.
SABLE IS A GIRL'S BEST FRIEND
Here, most women own at least one fur coat. The basic type is an astrakhan. Mink is considered expensive. Sable is even dearer and seen as a must for every wife or girlfriend of a newly-rich Russian.
Grisha's fur will fetch something between $150 and $200 after he is put down in December by lethal injection.
But you need many Grishas to make a coat. Alexander Zaidinov, director at Zoltikovsky, put the price of fur needed for a full-length coat at $2,800, excluding tailor's costs.
Zaidinov is in charge of some 1,000 people, 7,000 sables, dozens of lynx, about 10,000 foxes and other animals whose pelts can be turned into coats, blankets, hats or collars.

Hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of fur can be seen running, tossing and turning in the long rows of wire cages beyond trees and bushes in the well-kept farm, east of Moscow near the small town of Balashikha.

There are other signs that Zoltikovsky is not doing too badly. The workers are paid regularly -- not a usual practice in cash-strapped Russia where millions of people have to wait months for salaries and pensions.

The average wage is about 1.4 million roubles ($250), well above Russia's average monthly income of 850,000 roubles. A worker like Valentina, who looks after Grisha and other sables, feeds and sometimes cuddles them, gets about one million roubles.
"And we also pay taxes," said Zaidinov, indicating that his business must be relatively healthy. Many Russian firms do not pay their bills and evade taxes, saying they cannot afford to.
But the director said things were far from well. His farm, like others, was going through difficult times. "The situation is critical."
PRODUCTION COSTS RISING FASTER THAN REVENUE
Since the start of reforms in 1992, when many companies for the first time came across the concept of market prices, production costs in Russia rose faster than revenue.
Fur farms face the same problem. According to Russian estimates, the cost for producing one mink pelt rose 17-fold. Its price went up only nine-fold.

"Everything gets more expensive," Kovalyenko said. The farm imports some 20 percent of its animal food -- a greyish mix of fish, meat, cream cheese and dry food. "That is costly, but we do not get the same quality in Russia."

As a result of rising costs, Russian fur production has gone down, despite vast reserves of raw material. Mink production in 1996 dropped to some 3.2 million pelts from 4.8 million in 1995, according to Western estimates.

At the same time, Russia, a traditional seller on the world market, has become a major consumer. Ulrich Merget, head of the the Frankfurt-based German Fur Association, estimates that in 1996 Russia imported some 25 percent of world mink production -- about five million pelts.
Russian buyers regularly show up at international fur auctions and are now considered important clients.
"This is a sign that the Russian (consumer) market has clearly started to recover," Finnish fur auctioneer Turkistuottajat Oy said in April.

Fur coat production also dropped. In 1996 some 500,000 coats were made, down from 570,000 in 1995, the Russian State Statistical Agency said. Foreign coats, often from Greece and Turkey, fill the gap.

"They have modern technologies and produce better quality for a lower price than Russia", said Zaidinov. He has secured a Russian bank as an investor, which should provide him with access to credits, needed to upgrade the farm.

The people at Zoltikovsky have no moral qualms about their jobs. Valentina said her heart always ached when the sables were killed. "But look, they have a fine life. They get food, drink, we talk to them and when they feel unwell, we call the vet."
Russian animal activists, who are strictly against fur coats but lack money to organise protests, say domestic farms are keeping their animals properly.
"It's Russia which treats them most kindly," said Vera Maximova, vice-president of a Moscow-based animal protection society.
